Let me reconsider. Evidence:

Reading by column: c22: red s1, green s1; c28: green s2; c34: red s3, green s3; c40: red s4, green s4. Order: red s1, green s1, green s2, red s3, green s3, red s4, green s4 → O, p, R, b, N, Y, M: red s1=O ✓, green s1=p ✓, green s2=R, red s3=b, green s3=N, red s4=Y, green s4=M.
Or reading by row: red s1, s3, s4, green s1..s4: red s1=O ✓, red s3=p ✗ (rejected).
The column-wise hypothesis is consistent with all the evidence so far!
Targets: red s1=O ✓ (done), green s1=p ✓ (done), green s2=R, red s3=b, green s3=N, red s4=Y, green s4=M.
Hmm, but is column-wise reading natural? The chute at red s2 (c28) connects to the green tray... the chute is in column c28, which is green s2's column. Interesting.
Or the reading might be: red s1, green s1, red s3, green s2, red s4, green s3, green s4 (alternating red/green by column): O, p, R, b, N, Y, M → red s1=O, green s1=p, red s3=R, green s2=b, red s4=N, green s3=Y, green s4=M.
Both column-wise variants are consistent with the two data points. Ugh.
But actually, the simplest and most consistent rule is: "a piece can only be placed in a slot whose target matches the piece's color." This explains all the acceptances/rejections regardless of order. The target row order defines which slot gets which color, but I can determine the targets empirically by testing placements!

Variant 1 (column-wise, red-then-green within a column): red s1=O, green s1=p, green s2=R, red s3=b, green s3=N, red s4=Y, green s4=M.
Variant 2 (alternating): red s1=O, green s1=p, red s3=R, green s2=b, red s4=N, green s3=Y, green s4=M.
Hmm. Variant 1: the order is red s1, green s1, then green s2, red s3, green s3, red s4, green s4 — the order within column c28 is... wait, column c28 only has green s2 (red s2 is the chute).
